Guessing a Column's Type

guess-data-type.Rmd

The chooser above the detectors

The Data-Type Detector Guide describes the detector library: dozens of pure predicates that each answer one yes/no question about a column (is_currency_code(), is_iso_date(), is_county_fips(), …). guess_data_type() sits above them. Given a column of values it returns two aligned views: a v6 ontology $route — the current two-stage router → verifier answer — and a set of legacy detector fields kept for backward compatibility.

The $route: an ontology path, only as deep as it’s sure

$route anchors the column to the ontology (data_type › semantic_family › semantic_type › format_label; see the Data-Type Ontology vignette) and stops at the deepest coordinate the values actually support:

r <- guess_data_type(c("03/15/2019", "12/31/2020", "01/01/2021"))$route
r[c("data_type", "semantic_family", "semantic_type", "format_label",
    "match_kind", "depth", "confidence", "router_method")]
#> $data_type
#> [1] "temporal"
#> 
#> $semantic_family
#> [1] "date"
#> 
#> $semantic_type
#> [1] "calendar"
#> 
#> $format_label
#> [1] "calendar"
#> 
#> $match_kind
#> [1] "genome"
#> 
#> $depth
#> [1] 4
#> 
#> $confidence
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $router_method
#> [1] "learned"
  • depth records how far it resolved: 0 unknown · 1 data_type · 2 family · 3 semantic_type · 4 leaf (format). Fields below the confident depth are NA. A column of clean dates resolves all the way to a leaf; a column of ambiguous five-digit codes may stop at its data_type. This graceful truncation is deliberate — forcing a leaf would manufacture false precision.
  • match_kind is how the resolved type is recognized (genome / mask / lexicon / …).
  • router_method reports which router produced the shortlist (below).

Two stages: router, then verifier

  • Router (stage 1) shortlists candidate semantic types. Two ship: a learned xgboost model over the full value profile (fx_extract_features()), and a model-free signature router. The router = argument chooses ("auto", "learned", "signature"); with xgboost absent, "auto" falls back to the signature router.
  • Verifier (stage 2) confirms a leaf deterministically with confirm = detect ∘ transform, gated so that permissive types truncate instead of claiming a false leaf.
guess_data_type(c("14:30:00", "09:15:45", "23:59:59"),
                router = "signature")$route[c("semantic_type", "depth")]
#> $semantic_type
#> [1] "clock"
#> 
#> $depth
#> [1] 4

The legacy detector view

The same call also returns the flat detector fields it always did, so existing code keeps working:

g <- guess_data_type(c("USD", "EUR", "JPY", "GBP"))
g$guess
#> [1] "currency_code"
g$ontology
#>     data_type  data_subtype    data_class   data_format 
#> "categorical"     "nominal"    "category"        "code"
  • guess — the winning detector name, or NA when nothing is confident.
  • ontology — the flat c(data_type, data_subtype, data_class, data_format) coordinates for that detector (the legacy scheme; the v6 path is in $route).
  • confidence — the winner’s pass rate (share of values it matched).
  • candidates — every type that cleared the reporting floor, ranked.
  • n — how many unique values were actually scored.

The legacy path stays cheap on big data: it dedupes and samples (only unique non-missing values, at most n_sample, default 100), scores them against every registered detector, and ranks by pass rate. The raw scoring step is exposed on its own as score_data_type():

score_data_type(c("USD", "EUR", "XYZ"))[1, ]
#>       data_type n pass_rate
#> 1 currency_code 3 0.6666667

The name hint breaks ties the data can’t

Some values match more than one type. A five-digit code like 06037 is a valid ZIP and a valid county FIPS — both detectors pass at 100%. The data alone cannot choose; the variable name can (it is a tie-break for the legacy $guess):

vals <- c("06037", "36061", "48201", "17031")

guess_data_type(vals, name = "county_fips")$guess
#> [1] "county_fips"
guess_data_type(vals, name = "zip_code")$guess
#> [1] "zip_code"

Look at the ranked candidates to see why: both types pass at 1.0, so the name_match column casts the deciding vote, and with no name the tie falls to the more specific detector.

guess_data_type(vals, name = "county_fips")$candidates
#>     data_type n pass_rate name_match specific
#> 1 county_fips 4         1       TRUE    FALSE
#> 2    zip_code 4         1      FALSE     TRUE

Confidence, and the threshold / floor knobs

When nothing matches well, the honest answer is “I don’t know”:

guess_data_type(c("apple", "banana", "cherry"))$guess
#> [1] NA

Two thresholds control how bold the legacy guess is:

  • threshold (default 0.8) — the top type must match at least this share of values to be reported as guess; below it, guess is NA.
  • floor (default 0.5) — the minimum pass rate to appear in candidates.
# a column that is 3/4 ISO dates: unknown at the default, a date if you relax it
messy <- c("2016-03-15", "2016-03-13", "1999-12-31", "not a date")
guess_data_type(messy)$guess               # NA (below 0.8)
#> [1] NA
guess_data_type(messy, threshold = 0.7)$guess
#> [1] "iso_date"

From a guess to a stable column

Because $route returns the ontology semantic_type and format_label, its output hands straight to fx_stabilize() to normalize the column:

x     <- c("03/15/2019", "12/31/2020", "01/01/2021")
route <- guess_data_type(x)$route
fx_stabilize(x, route$semantic_type, route$format_label)$stable
#> [1] "2019-03-15" "2020-12-31" "2021-01-01"

That is the whole formex loop: guess_data_type() says what a column is, and fx_stabilize() puts it in a standard form. A downstream workflow package (such as datagoodr) can build a per-column governance file on top of these two calls — see the Data-Type Ontology vignette for the coordinates they share.
